claim: The U.S. surgeon general and the Centers for Disease Control both previously said that ‘masks are not effective in preventing [the] general public from catching coronavirus.’
justification: Multiple independent news sources (Bloomberg, CNN, The Hill, Time, CBS News, Wikipedia) confirm that Surgeon General Jerome Adams tweeted on Feb 29, 2020 that masks 'are NOT effective in preventing general public from catching Coronavirus,' explicitly citing CDC guidance, and that the CDC itself did not recommend masks for healthy members of the public at that time. This was official U.S. government messaging from Feb-March 2020, before it was reversed on April 3, 2020.

claim: Joe Biden wants to ban fracking
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (CNN, AP, NBC, Washington Post, Newsweek) from the exact time period found that Biden's actual written policy only proposed banning new oil and gas permits on federal public lands, not a nationwide fracking ban, and that Biden repeatedly and explicitly denied wanting to ban fracking. While Biden's past primary-debate comments created genuine confusion that partially justified the attack, fact-checkers consistently rated the blanket claim that 'Biden wants to ban fracking' as false or misleading.

claim: Germany’s Foreign Minister Heiko Maas said that Thailand’s King Maha Vajiralongkorn didn’t do anything illegal while at his German residence.
justification: On 26-27 October 2020, Maas's actual public remarks were cautionary — he said Germany was monitoring the King's activities and that illegal conduct 'would have immediate consequences,' not that the King had done nothing illegal. The clear statement that the King 'had not done anything illegal' was issued by the German Government in November 2020, weeks after the claimed date, and was not a direct personal statement from Maas but a government response to a protester letter.

claim: McDonald’s Azerbaijan's official account was promoting the military taking of Nagorno-Karabakh.
justification: Multiple independent outlets (VOA/Polygraph.info, Washington Post, CTV News, Business and Human Rights Centre, JAMnews) confirm that McDonald's Azerbaijan's official social media accounts posted pro-military, pro-Azerbaijan content about Nagorno-Karabakh around Oct 27, 2020, which was later deleted after backlash. The specific quoted tweet text matches what was reported as originating on Twitter that same day, and McDonald's Corporation itself confirmed to press that its Azerbaijan franchisee had removed the content.

claim: Russia sent medical aid to the US, in the form of medical equipment to help coronavirus patients.
justification: Multiple independent, contemporaneous news sources (Reuters via The Hill, Moscow Times, AP via Courthouse News, Boston Globe, Fox News, NPR) confirm that Russia did send medical equipment (ventilators, masks, protective gear) to the US in April 2020 to help with the coronavirus response, and that Peskov made statements confirming this. The core factual claim is well-substantiated, though the full story is more nuanced (partial US payment, faulty/unusable ventilators later discarded). I could not locate the specific October 21, 2020 RIA Novosti article to confirm the exact wording of Peskov's statement on that date, but the underlying fact he would have been referencing is well-documented.

claim: India's imports from China increased by 27% during the period April-August 2020.
justification: Multiple sources, including a PIB Fact Check response and government data from Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal's statement to Parliament, confirm that India's imports from China actually DECREASED by 27.63% during April-August 2020, while it was India's EXPORTS to China that increased by 27% during that period. Pachauri appears to have conflated imports and exports, and later posted a partial correction acknowledging the error while still maintaining a broader point about trade dynamics.

claim: Prominent US Democrat party members including Hillary and Bill Clinton, were running a child sex-trafficking ring in the basement of a Washington, D.C., pizzeria.
justification: This is the thoroughly debunked 'Pizzagate' conspiracy theory. Multiple independent investigations by law enforcement (DC Metropolitan Police called it 'fictitious'), major news organizations (NYT, Washington Post, CNN, Fox News), and fact-checkers (Snopes) found no evidence supporting the claim. Critically, Comet Ping Pong has no basement at all, directly contradicting the core physical claim, and the 'evidence' cited by proponents was traced to misread emails and unrelated photos.

claim: India's Congress party candidate Maskoor Usmani installed Jinnah's portrait at AMU.
justification: Multiple independent fact-checks (Alt News via Pooja Chaudhuri, republished by NewsClick, The Wire, and National Herald) explicitly debunked this exact claim on the exact date cited. Aaj Tak's TV claim that Usmani 'installed' Jinnah's portrait was found false — the portrait has hung at AMU since 1938, decades before Usmani was born, and he was only involved in opposing its removal in 2018, not installing it. Usmani himself denied the installation claim as 'false propaganda.'

claim: Donald Trump is facing a court case for raping a teen in 1994
justification: A 1994 rape allegation lawsuit against Trump (the 'Jane Doe'/'Katie Johnson' case, filed 2016) did exist, but it was withdrawn by the plaintiff in early November 2016 and never refiled — four years before this October 2020 claim. Multiple sources (Wikipedia, PBS, Newsweek) confirm the case was dropped in November 2016 and no active court case on this matter existed by October 2020, making the claim of Trump 'facing a court case' at that time inaccurate.

claim: Charlotta Bass was the first Black woman to run for vice president in 1952
justification: Multiple independent and authoritative sources — including PBS, the National Park Service, Britannica, Wikipedia, the Washington Post, and Democracy Now — consistently confirm that Charlotta Bass ran as the Progressive Party's vice-presidential candidate in 1952, making her the first Black woman to run for vice president of the United States. This fact was widely reported in mainstream media in August 2020, shortly before the claim in question was made.

claim: Senate President Vicente Sotto III claimed that hardheaded Filipinos are to blame for the cases of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) in the country
justification: Manila Bulletin's October 3, 2020 report directly quotes Sotto attributing the Philippines' high COVID-19 case ranking to Filipino 'stubbornness'/hardheadedness rather than solely government failures, matching the claim precisely. This is corroborated by VERA Files, a Philippine fact-checking organization, which explicitly fact-checked this exact claim ('Senate President claimed that hardheaded Filipinos are to blame for the cases of COVID-19') and rated it as without basis, confirming both the statement was made and its date.

claim: US President Donald Trump's positive COVID-19 result is a false positive, which could allow an adversary in the White House to poison the president’s soda and later say that he suffered from COVID-19.
justification: The Media Matters article (dated October 2, 2020) directly quotes Alex Jones making this exact claim on his show: that the COVID test was a 'false positive' and that someone in the White House could 'poison his Diet Coke or something, he gets really sick and they said it's COVID-19.' This is corroborated by a Vice article describing Jones's broader, related conspiracy theory about Trump's Diet Coke being poisoned.

claim: For a cumulative 29 of Nigeria's 60 years of existence as a nation, it has been under military rule.’
justification: Multiple independent primary sources, including the official Channels Television full-text transcript, the Nigerian State House website, and several other major news outlets (Vanguard, Guardian, TheCable, TVC News), all reproduce the identical verbatim quote from Buhari's October 1, 2020 Independence Day address: 'For a cumulative 29 of our 60 years existence as a nation, we have been under military rule.' This matches the claim exactly in wording, speaker, date, and context.

claim: Fuel in Nigeria in 2020 was not cheaper than that in Saudi Arabia.
justification: Multiple independent news outlets (Vanguard, BusinessDay, TheCable, Guardian Nigeria, Nairametrics) reporting on Buhari's actual October 1, 2020 speech confirm he stated Nigerian petrol sold at N161/litre versus N168/litre in Saudi Arabia, explicitly arguing it made no sense for fuel to be cheaper in Nigeria than Saudi Arabia. Africa Check's independent fact-check using GlobalPetrolPrices.com data also found Nigeria's prices were broadly lower than Saudi Arabia's at that time. This directly contradicts the claim that Nigerian fuel was 'not cheaper' than Saudi Arabia's in 2020.

claim: Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said ‘our job is to save cows, not women.’
justification: No primary source, transcript, or reputable news report was found confirming Yogi Adityanath ever said 'our job is to save cows, not women.' Search results instead show PTI Fact Check specifically flagging 'viral video misquotes Yogi Adityanath' content, and actual verified statements from him around this period are about cow protection resolve, not a direct comparison devaluing women's safety. The claim's attribution to a Twitter user rather than a news outlet also fits the pattern of unverified social media paraphrasing rather than a documented quote.

claim: Amy Coney Barrett has a written track record, disagreeing adamantly with the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision to uphold the Affordable Care Act.
justification: The Hill's contemporaneous September 27, 2020 report directly quotes Biden citing Barrett's 'written track record of disagreeing adamantly' with Supreme Court rulings upholding the ACA. This is corroborated by extensive independent reporting (NBC News, CNN, CNBC, CBS News) confirming Barrett's 2017 Notre Dame law review article criticized Chief Justice Roberts' reasoning in NFIB v. Sebelius (2012) that upheld the ACA, and that she wrote favorably of Scalia's dissents in both that case and King v. Burwell (2015).

claim: Fact Check: WHO has not approved home remedy for COVID-19, don’t fall for misinformation
justification: The substantive claim that WHO never approved any COVID-19 home remedy is well-supported by multiple independent fact-checks (PIB Fact Check, South Asia Check/The Record Nepal) from the same period, which debunked viral WhatsApp/Facebook messages claiming WHO approval of home remedies like black pepper-honey-ginger mixtures. A LinkedIn profile confirms a Sonali Khatta works professionally in COVID-related health fact-checking, making the attribution plausible, but I could not directly locate the specific tweet dated 21 September 2020 to confirm exact authorship and wording.

claim: Muslim candidates can qualify with lower marks than others in the UPCS (i.e. Union Public Service Commission for recruitment to higher Civil Services of the Government of India) exam
justification: Multiple fact-checks (notably The Wire's detailed rebuttal of Sudarshan News' 'UPSC Jihad' show) found that UPSC's published cut-off marks and attempt limits are differentiated by reserved category (SC/ST/OBC) status, not religion, and that UPSC notifications explicitly do not permit religion-based relaxation. The claim conflates caste/category-based reservations with religion, and India's Information & Broadcasting Ministry itself flagged this and related claims from the show as misleading.

claim: Since 2002, South Africa’s police force has grown by 50%.
justification: Africa Check's fact-check (14 Sept 2020) directly examined this claim using SAPS annual reports and found actual growth of 45.3% (total staff, 2002/03 vs 2018/19) or 47% (police-only personnel, UN definition), concluding the 50% claim was 'mostly correct.' The figure is a close, if slightly rounded-up, approximation of verified official SAPS data.

claim: The Obama-Biden administration secretly launched a surveillance operation on the Trump campaign.
justification: Grenell did say this exact line at the RNC on Aug 26, 2020 (confirmed by transcript and multiple outlets), but the substantive claim — that Obama and Biden 'secretly launched a surveillance operation' on the Trump campaign — was extensively fact-checked as false by CNN, NBC, and The Washington Post (which gave it 'four Pinocchios'). The DOJ Inspector General found no evidence of political bias behind the FBI's Crossfire Hurricane investigation, and reviews found no evidence Obama or Biden personally ordered surveillance of Trump campaign aides.
